vessels.name: Dugout canoe
rows: Sugime, 7.6 m cedar: Taiwan→Yonaguni, 225 km in 45 h ≈ 2.5–3 kn
vessels.text:
No watercraft survives from the crossing to Sahul. That people arrived is certain; what they arrived in is not, and this model does not draw the vessel.

What the record does support is a negative: **bamboo rafts do not work.** Kaifu's experimental crossings (National Museum of Nature and Science, Tokyo, 2016–19) found rafts made under a knot against the 1–2 knot Kuroshio and failed outright, while a 7.6 m cedar dugout crossed 225 km of open water in 45 hours. If the Pleistocene sea craft was anything, it was more like a dugout than a raft.

The date is itself contested: Madjedbebe's optically stimulated luminescence gives 65 ± 6 ka (Clarkson et al., *Nature*, 2017); Allen and O'Connell argue for ~50 ka.
vessels.cite: Clarkson et al. 2017; Kealy, Louys & O'Connor 2018; Kaifu experimental crossings 2016–19.

polar.rigNote: Paddled. The one measured figure is a crossing, not a sprint: a 7.6 m cedar dugout took 225 km of the Kuroshio, Taiwan to Yonaguni, in 45 hours — very close to 3 kn held for two days, and that is the paddling floor the router holds in any wind, including a calm. The rise off the wind is the fair-wind mat sail of the Pacific logboats (Haddon & Hornell), set only when the wind serves; no mast is drawn, and none is attested this early.
polar.rig: paddles, with a mat sail for fair winds

anchor.source: Kaifu's Sugime crossing 2019: 225 km in 45 h ≈ 3 kn; Haddon & Hornell, Canoes of Oceania, for the fair-wind sail

floor.source: Kaifu's Sugime crossing for the floor. No measured logboat headwind figure exists; the loss is Olympias's fractional windage (46% of floor at 8 m/s) carried over — an inference, stated as one

vessels.name: Voyaging canoe
rows: 18.7 m LOA · 4.72 m beam · 0.76 m draught
**two masts**, crab claw — a triangular sail on two spars along its long sides
a long paddle, not a rudder
Hawaiʻi→Tahiti 1976, ~2,400 nm in 30 days at sea ≈ 3.3 kn
lashed-lug planking, no metal at all
vessels.text:
A double-hulled sailing canoe: two hulls of equal length lashed side by side, carrying two masts and steered by a long paddle rather than a rudder. Austronesian voyagers using vessels of this kind settled the Pacific islands, reaching the Lapita range by about 900 BC and Hawaiʻi, Rapa Nui and Aotearoa later.

The crab claw is approximately an isosceles triangle carried on two light spars along its long sides. It generates lift rather than merely catching wind, and it **widens upwards**, putting sail area high where the wind is stronger — which also raises the heeling moment, and is why the rig is carried on a multihull. A double hull carries enough sail to use it, and the combination makes good about 75° to the true wind, against roughly 90° for a square rig in ordinary conditions.

Lashed-lug construction uses planks carved with integral internal lugs and lashed to ribs with fibre — no nails, no iron, nothing that corrodes.
vessels.cite: Irwin, *Archaeology in Oceania* 58 (2023); Finney, *Science* (1977); Polynesian Voyaging Society logs.

polar.rigNote: Poor by modern standards, positive by ancient ones — and positive is the whole argument, because it is what lets a canoe beat back the way she came. Fastest on a broad reach, not before the wind.
polar.rig: crab claw on a double hull

anchor.source: Finney, Hōkūleʻa Hawaiʻi→Tahiti 1976: ~100 nm/day, best days near 7 kn

vessels.text:
A hull built to carry a bronze ram at speed and to turn inside its own length. It is also the best-measured ancient ship in existence, because one was built.

*Olympias* (1987) **fell short of what the ancient sources imply**, and the shortfall is the interesting part. Xenophon implies 7–8 knots sustained for sixteen hours; the reconstruction managed 8.3 knots for a sprint and about 5.4 sustained. Coates concluded the hull is roughly 10% overweight and too short — Vitruvius's two-cubit oar spacing at the longer Ionic cubit gives a hull over 40 m, and a Mark II on those lines was calculated to reach 9.7 kn sprint and 7.5 sustained. It has never been built.

The widely repeated 8.9 knots was a single momentary GPS reading; the Final Report says 8.3 kn is the honest figure, 'achieved only momentarily (if at all)'.
vessels.cite: Rankov (ed.), *Trireme Olympias: The Final Report* (Oxbow, 2012); Morrison, Coates & Rankov, *The Athenian Trireme*.

polar.rigNote: A galley goes where it likes and not far, and the figure above is her SAILING speed — the sail is for fair winds only. Under oar: 8.3 kn sprint, 5.4 kn cruise, and about 2.9 kn into a headwind with a metre of sea — measured on the reconstruction Olympias, which fell short of what the ancient sources imply and is thought to be ~10% too short in the hull. The router holds the 5.4 as her oar floor in any wind, falling to the measured 2.9 dead upwind in a fresh breeze.
polar.rig: oars, with a square sail for fair winds

anchor.source: Olympias Final Report: 8.3 kn "achieved only momentarily", cruise 5.4 under oar

floor.source: Olympias sea trials: 5.4 kn oar cruise; ~2.9 kn into a head sea at force 4–5, taken at the polar's 8 m/s reference — (5.4 − 2.9)/8

vessels.name: Roman merchantman
rows: one mainmast with a broad square mainsail; larger ships carried more than one mast and more than one sail per mast — the raked *artemon* forward and a triangular *supparum* above the main (Casson)
no reef points: brailing lines ran through lead or bone rings sewn to the sail and gathered it up to the yard
55 m; beam over a quarter of that; hold 13 m deep; 1,200–1,300 t of grain (Lucian) — contested, some read 1,900 t
Alexandria→Rome laden a month, sometimes two or more
about 70 days; 2,000–3,000 voyages a year fed the city
vessels.text:
The bulk carrier of the Roman Mediterranean, built shell-first with pegged mortise-and-tenon joints and double planking. Typical hulls ran 20–30 m and carried 150–350 tons; the standard grain capacity was 50,000 *modii*, about 350 tonnes.

The rig is a single broad square mainsail on one mast, with a small raked *artemon* over the bows on larger ships and sometimes a triangular *supparum* above the main. It was handled by **brailing**: there are no reef points, and the yard does not come down. Lines ran up the face of the sail through rings of lead or bone sewn to the cloth, and hauling on them gathered the sail up to the yard like a curtain.

The same ship on the same route took ten days to a fortnight in one direction and a month or more in the other. The difference is the wind: the Etesian northerlies of the eastern Mediterranean blow steadily down toward Egypt in summer. The grain fleet ran downwind to Alexandria in ballast and beat its way home laden, a round trip of about seventy days, and the sailing season closed in winter when the *mare clausum* held from November to March.
vessels.cite: Casson, *Ships and Seamanship in the Ancient World* (1971); Lucian, *The Ship*; Wikipedia, *Grain supply to the city of Rome* and *Square rig* (accessed 2026-08-02).

polar.rigNote: The famous "six points" is 67.5° — and it is a HEADING. What she makes good is the figure above, and above force 4 she loses ground to leeward faster than she gains it.

anchor.source: Casson, Ships and Seamanship: Puteoli→Alexandria ~9 d fair; favorable runs 4.5–6 kn

vessels.name: Sewn-plank dhow
rows: one to three masts carrying **settee** sails — a quadrilateral, a lateen with its forward point cut off — sometimes a true lateen
*baghlah* the heavy deep-sea trader · *boum* large, tapering stern · *sambuk* the largest still sailing in the Gulf · *jalibut* small to medium
about 30 on a large dhow, about 12 on a small one
coir stitching through drilled holes; no iron
out on the SW monsoon Apr–Sep, home on the NE Nov–Mar
vessels.text:
A sewn-plank trader of one to three masts. The sail is usually a **settee** rather than a true lateen: a quadrilateral, in effect a lateen with its forward point cut off, so the luff is short and the yard still rakes steeply.

In the Indian Ocean the departure **date** is not a free variable. The monsoon reverses twice a year, and it is the only wind system on Earth that does, so the calendar of the whole ocean is fixed by it: Egypt to India leaving in July on the south-west monsoon, home from November on the north-east.

The *Periplus of the Erythraean Sea* states the month outright — 'about the month of July, that is Epiphi' — four separate times, for four separate routes.

Sewn construction with no iron at all was not primitive. It flexed on a reef instead of splitting, and it could be repaired anywhere there was coir.
vessels.cite: *Periplus Maris Erythraei* §§14, 24, 39, 49, 56; Flecker on the Belitung wreck.

polar.rigNote: Better than a square rig, and by less than the textbooks claim — their 55–65° is a heading. The cost is manpower: tacking means walking the whole yard round the mast.

anchor.source: Villiers, Sons of Sindbad: monsoon day's runs ~130 nm

vessels.text:
A seagoing hull with watertight transverse bulkheads, an axial sternpost rudder and the magnetic compass used at sea, each attested in China well before it appeared in Europe. The hull descends from tapering rafts rather than from the dugout.

⚠ The battened lug is the exception and is often miscounted among them. Junks carried square sails until about the 12th century and then adopted the tanja sail and the fully battened rig from the southern seas. The battens make the sail self-reefing and allow it to set flat. A junk therefore works to windward considerably better than a square rig, and with a smaller crew: reefing is done by lowering battens onto the boom from the deck. Instrumented comparisons put a junk at 75–80% of a Bermudan rig's windward performance.
vessels.cite: Needham, *Science and Civilisation in China* IV.3; Quanzhou ship excavation 1974; Junk Rig Association instrumented polars.

vessels.name: Treasure ship
vessels.sub: 寶船 — and how big it really was

vessels.text:
**The famous dimensions come from a novel.** The 44-zhang figure appears first in Luo Maodeng's *Xiyang Ji* of 1597 — a work of fiction written 164 years after the last voyage, in which ships are built with divine assistance — and was carried into the *Ming Shi* when that was compiled in 1739.

Two physical arguments cut against it. A length-to-beam ratio of 2.5 is a barge, not a seagoing hull; and unreinforced wooden hulls hog beyond about 90 m, which is why the longest wooden ship ever built needed iron strapping and still leaked continuously. Then the decisive one: the Longjiang shipyard was excavated in 2003–04 and its largest building basin is **421 m long and 41 m wide** — narrower than the 52 m beam the ships are supposed to have had.

The hull drawn here is at the defensible length. The claimed length is shown as an outline beside it, because the claim is part of the history even though it is almost certainly wrong.
vessels.cite: Church, *Monumenta Serica* 53 (2005); Sleeswyk, *Nautical Research Journal* (1996); Xin Yuan'ou; Longjiang shipyard excavation 2003–04.

rows: 74–76° made good in a gentle breeze; LOSES ground in 20 kn

vessels.text:
Flat-bottomed so it could take the ground on a tidal flat and be unloaded at low water, which is what the Hanse ports needed. It also carries the **pintle-and-gudgeon stern rudder**, first depicted on the Winchester font about 1180 — the single most important European ship fitting of the Middle Ages.

A replica was instrumented and the result is sobering: in a gentle breeze it made good 74–76° to the true wind with a velocity made good of 0.15 knots. In twenty knots of wind it lost ground.
vessels.cite: Bremen cog, Deutsches Schiffahrtsmuseum; Brandt & Hochkirch 1995 replica trials.

vessels.name: Caravel
rows: about 3.5 : 1 - fine for its date, and most of why it was fast and handy
caravela LATINA, lateen throughout; caravela REDONDA, a square foremast with lateen masts abaft it
15-20 m, beam about 6 m, 60-75 tons displacement
carvel - the word descends through Byzantine Greek karabos, a light ship
vessels.text:
A small, shallow, weatherly hull carrying two or three lateen sails. Its significance is its ability to sail to windward: a square-rigged cog could run down to Guinea on the north-east trades but could not return against them, whereas a caravel could work back.

What it made possible has a name: the ***volta do mar***, the turn of the sea. To come home from West Africa you do not beat up the coast against the trades. You stand out **west** into the middle of the Atlantic, as far as the Azores, pick up the westerlies at 35–40°N and run home on them. Sailing away from your destination in order to reach it is the first great piece of applied knowledge about the wind field, and in 1500 Cabral's southern version of it swung so far west that it reached Brazil.
vessels.cite: Portuguese *Regimento* c. 1509; Barros, *Décadas da Ásia*.

anchor.source: Columbus's 1492 Diario: best day's run ~182 nm in the trades

vessels.text:
A three- or four-masted ocean-going ship developed in Portugal and Spain during the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries, carvel-built, with a forecastle forward and a high rounded stern carrying an aftcastle. It carried cargo and guns on the same voyage and was large enough to remain stable in heavy seas.

The rig is mixed: square sails on the fore and main for driving power, a lateen mizzen aft to help the ship steer and lie closer to the wind. A typical three-master set six sails — spritsail, foresail, mainsail, mizzen and two topsails.

Portuguese carracks on the India run were often over 1,000 tons. Galleons gradually superseded the type from the late sixteenth century, though carracks remained in use into the middle of the seventeenth.
vessels.cite: Rodrigues & Loureiro on the *carreira da Índia*; Wikipedia, *Carrack* (accessed 2026-08-02).

vessels.text:
The standard Mediterranean warship for four hundred years after gunpowder, and the ship that fought Lepanto — about 400 of them on one afternoon in October 1571, the largest galley action ever fought.

Her armament faces FORWARD. The heavy gun sits on the centreline at the bow, aimed by aiming the ship, and it fired once — at fifty metres or less, immediately before boarding. The broadside that was re-organising Atlantic warfare in the same century has no place here: the sides are full of oars.

The dimensions of a fighting fact: 42 m of hull carries only 1.1 m of freeboard, so the rowing frame — the *apostis*, the rectangular outrigger the oars actually pivot on — stands wider than the hull itself, and the spur at the bow is a boarding bridge, not a ram. At Lepanto the two systems of rowing met: Venice still rowed *alla sensile*, three separate oars to a bench; Spain and Genoa had gone *a scaloccio*, one great oar pulled by three to five men. Everyone converted after the battle, because a scaloccio can be rowed by chained men and sensile cannot.

Guilmartin's central measurement is logistical: a galley dashes at 7 knots for twenty minutes, cruises at 3–4, and carries water for a few days at most — 150 rowers working in a Mediterranean summer drink tons of it. Galley war is therefore amphibious war, fought port to port along coasts, and it ended not when sailing ships got better guns but when the round ship could finally keep the sea in winter.
vessels.cite: Guilmartin, *Gunpowder and Galleys* (rev. ed., Naval Institute Press, 2003); Morrison (ed.), *The Age of the Galley* (Conway, 1995).

polar.rigNote: The figures above are her SAILING speed in a moderate breeze, lateen canvas on both masts — passage-making rig, struck and sent ashore before battle, and a poor sailer even so: the hull is built for oars, shallow and leeway-prone. In strong fair winds the router lets the curve saturate at her recorded 7.2 kn. Under oars: a dash of just over 7 kn held for perhaps twenty minutes, cruise 3–4 kn (Guilmartin). The router holds 3.5 kn as her oar floor in any wind. No instrumented galley trial exists; the headwind loss is carried over from Olympias's measured ratio, scaled to this cruise.
polar.rig: oars, with two lateen masts for passage

anchor.source: Guilmartin, Gunpowder and Galleys: a dash of just over 7 kn, sustainable for about twenty minutes; cruise 3–4 kn under oars

floor.source: cruise per Guilmartin; headwind loss inferred from Olympias's measured (5.4−2.9)/8, scaled to a 3.5 kn cruise — no instrumented galley trial exists

rows: ~47 m; about 51 m over the spur
~8 m; about 9.4 m over the rowing frame

perhaps 600 t loaded — three times a war galley
about 2.8 m to the gun deck, against a galley's 1.1 — her deck must be climbed, not stepped onto
26 benches a side, one great oar to a bench, five or more men on each
about 3 kn, briefly; at Lepanto each was towed into position by two galleys

vessels.text:
A merchant great galley's hull converted into a floating battery — the heaviest thing under oars in the sixteenth-century Mediterranean, and the type that opened Lepanto. Venice built her out of the reserve of galee grosse, the three-masted merchant galleys that had carried the Flanders and Levant trades, and the six that the Arsenal finished converting in 1570–71 fought at the front of the Christian line on 7 October 1571.

Structurally she inverts the war galley's one hard constraint. A galia sottile carries her whole battery at the bow because her sides at gun height are full of oars. The great galley's hull is deep enough to carry a second deck clear over the rowers' heads, spanning the full width of the rowing frame, and the guns stand on that deck and fire outboard over the oars — eight or nine pieces a side, with the five-piece heavy battery at the bow and chasers aft, about thirty guns in all. Her freeboard, about 2.8 m to the gun deck against a galley's 1.1, means a galley alongside cannot board her without climbing.

At Lepanto the six galleasses were towed into position in pairs ahead of the Christian line, and the Ottoman fleet had to row past them to come to grips. Their fire — the first sustained heavy-gun bombardment an Ottoman galley fleet had ever taken from shipboard — sank or damaged a number of galleys and, what mattered more, broke up the dressing of the Ottoman line before contact. Guilmartin's judgment is that the galleasses did not win the battle by gunfire; they disordered the attack that the Christian galleys then destroyed at close quarters.

She was too heavy to row effectively — about three knots in a burst, towed whenever the fleet manoeuvred — and depended on her lateen rig for passage. Spain sent four galleasses of the Naples squadron with the 1588 Armada, where one, Girona, was wrecked on the Antrim coast with some 1,300 men lost. Venice kept galleasses in commission into the early eighteenth century, but the broadside's future belonged to the pure sailing ship, which carried more guns further on a fraction of the crew.
vessels.cite: Guilmartin, *Gunpowder and Galleys* (rev. ed., Naval Institute Press, 2003); Morrison (ed.), *The Age of the Galley* (Conway, 1995).

polar.rigNote: The figures are her SAILING speed in a moderate breeze, three lateens standing — the war galley's own lateen curve shape, scaled down for a hull of three times the displacement on barely more canvas per ton. Under oars she is the slowest fighting ship of her century: about 3 kn in a burst, and at Lepanto each galleass was towed into position by two galleys so the rowers would arrive fresh. No instrumented galleass trial exists; every oar figure here is inference and labelled so.

rows: ~32 m for a large ship; medium ships about 21 m
~9.4 m — length to beam about 3.4, against a Mediterranean galley's 8.1

about 2 m to the gunwale, 3.6 m to the fighting deck — a boarder must climb two storeys

vessels.text:
The standard warship of the Joseon navy from 1555 until the nineteenth century, and the ship Yi Sun-sin fought every battle of the Imjin War with. The name means "board-roofed ship": above the oar deck the shipwrights built a second, higher deck on stanchions — the sangjang — walled with heavy plank, so that the whole fighting crew stands a full storey above the water behind timber, with the commander's roofed tower rising amidships. The first was launched in 1555, after the Eulmyo wako raid of that year showed the old single-decked ships could be boarded and taken.

Her construction is the Korean coastal tradition scaled up to war burden. The bottom is dead flat, built of thick pine planks edge-fastened with oak pegs and locked by massive crossbeams whose ends pierce the hull sides — no iron nails, and no keel. A flat bottom suits a coast with some of the world's largest tides: she takes the ground upright when the water leaves, and she turns nearly in her own length, pivoting on it. The price is speed. Fifty to sixty rowers working eight to ten great sculling oars drove perhaps three knots, and both fleets' accounts agree the Japanese ships were faster through the water.

The two navies of the Imjin War (1592–1598) disagreed about what a warship is for. The Japanese fleet — atakebune and the lighter sekibune — carried arquebusiers and swordsmen, and fought by coming alongside and boarding; its lightly framed hulls mounted few heavy guns, because they could not bear the recoil. The panokseon is the opposite argument built in timber: heavy cannon — the cheonja, jija, hyeonja and hwangja chongtong, throwing iron shot and the great fletched daejanggunjeon to several hundred metres — worked from behind a high plank bulwark that boarders would have to climb. Joseon squadrons stood off, fired, and dismasted or holed the boarders before they could close. The geobukseon, the famous turtle ship, is this same hull with the fighting deck roofed over completely.

Her hardest test came after her navy was nearly destroyed. At Chilcheollyang in August 1597 a Joseon fleet under Won Gyun was annihilated — and thirteen panokseon survived. With those thirteen, reinstated to command, Yi Sun-sin met the Japanese advance fleet of 133 warships in the Myeongnyang strait on 26 October 1597, where a tidal race runs to ten knots and reverses. Anchored across the narrows against the flood, his line fought until the tide turned, then drove the disordered Japanese van back through the strait onto their own supports. About thirty Japanese ships were destroyed; no panokseon was lost. The type, continued as the jeonseon of the late Joseon fleet, remained the kingdom's standard warship until the navy itself was reorganised out of existence in the 1890s.
vessels.cite: Hong Sun-jae, 'Understanding the Structure of the Panokseon' (*Military History* 135, 2025); Hawley, *The Imjin War* (RAS Korea, 2005); Underwood, *Korean Boats and Ships* (1934). No panokseon survives; every dimension here is a reconstruction from the documentary record and is labelled derived where it is inference.

polar.rigNote: The figures are her SAILING speed in a moderate breeze, both battened lugs standing — the junk-family curve shape (the Korean sail is the same engineering: a balanced lug held flat by full-length battens), scaled down for a flat-bottomed hull of war burden that makes leeway freely. No Joseon log records a measured passage speed; the anchor is derived and labelled so. Under oars: about 3 kn, 50–60 rowers on eight to ten sculls — both fleets' battle accounts agree the Japanese ships were faster, which is the only speed attestation that exists. vessels.text:
The standard warship of Japan from the Sengoku wars to the end of the Edo bakufu. The name means "barrier ship": the ships that enforced the toll barriers (seki) the lords of the Inland Sea — above all the Murakami houses — maintained across their straits, stopping, taxing and if need be taking every hull that passed. A navy's ships were counted by their oars: under forty a kobaya, a scout and messenger; forty to eighty a sekibune; above that, with beam to carry a castle, an atakebune. The sekibune is the cruiser of the three — a long, narrow hull on a single sharp stem, lightly framed, shallow, and by every account of the Imjin War faster through the water than anything Korea sent against her.

Her construction is the Japanese coastal tradition put to war. A wasen carries no keel: a heavy flat bottom plank, broad side strakes edge-fastened with iron staples and nails, crossbeams whose ends pierce the planking, a square stern with a great hanging median rudder that can be raised in shoal water, and the sharp raked stem — a single plank, the mizu-oshi — that parts the water. Over nearly the whole length of the hull the shipwrights laid the sō-yagura, a full fighting deck, and walled it with tate-ita, shield planks pierced by sama — loopholes for bows and arquebuses. The single mast is unstepped before action and laid down the yagura roof, and the ship fights under her forty sculling ro alone, one man standing at each.

Her doctrine was the opposite of the panokseon's, and the two argued it out across the Imjin War (1592–1598). A sekibune's light frame cannot bear the recoil of heavy cannon, so she carried almost none: her weapons were the arquebus through the loophole and the grappling iron over the rail, and her speed existed to close the range and put swordsmen on the enemy's deck. Against Chinese and Korean coasters, and in the fleet actions of the Inland Sea, it worked. Against a Joseon line that stood off behind high timber and fired cannon, it mostly did not. At Myeongnyang on 26 October 1597 the tidal race barred the deep atakebune, so the 133 warships that entered the strait were led by sekibune — and thirteen panokseon anchored across the narrows destroyed about thirty of them, killing the fleet's van commander Kurushima Michifusa, without losing a ship.

The type outlived the war by two and a half centuries, because the Tokugawa peace was built partly on its back. In 1609 the shogunate confiscated every atakebune in Japan and capped the daimyo at ships of 500 koku, which made the sekibune the largest warship a lord could own; the great houses built them to the limit, lacquered and gilded them into gozabune, and rowed their lords to Edo in them on the alternate-attendance processions. The shogun's own, the red-lacquered Tenchi-maru of 1630 — 500 koku, 76 oars — served for 230 years and was broken up only in the 1860s, when the navy that replaced her class ran on steam.
vessels.cite: Turnbull, Fighting Ships of the Far East (2): Japan and Korea AD 612–1639 (Osprey, 2003); Hawley, The Imjin War (RAS Korea, 2005); Museum of Maritime Science, Tokyo (Tenchi-maru); the Busan boat-barrier scroll of 1593 (Univ. of Tokyo), the card's own plate. No Sengoku sekibune survives; the classification by oar count is recorded, and every dimension here is a reconstruction from it, labelled derived where it is inference.

vessels.text:
A cargo vessel designed by shipwrights of Hoorn in the Dutch Republic in the 1590s and built to no other purpose. The hull is pear-shaped in section, broad in the hold and narrow at the deck, with a shallow draught that let it reach ports and rivers closed to deeper ships. Armament was minimised or omitted to leave the hold clear, which restricted it to waters where it did not expect to fight.

It was built of softwood cut by wind-powered sawmills and rigged so that twelve to fifteen men could work it where an English ship of the same burden needed about thirty. It carried roughly twice the cargo of its rivals at about half the freight cost.

⚠ The narrow deck is often explained as evasion of the Danish Sound Toll, which is said to have been charged on deck area. **The Sound Toll Registers do not support it**: officers assessed dues from the bills of lading a master presented, not from any measurement of the ship. The shape follows from what the hull is for — hold volume below, and as little weight and rigging as possible above.
vessels.cite: Unger, *Dutch Shipbuilding before 1800*; Sound Toll Registers Online; Wikipedia, *Fluyt* (accessed 2026-08-02).

vessels.text:
A three-masted armed merchantman chartered by the European East India companies for the Asia trade: the British EIC from 1600 to 1834, the Dutch VOC through the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, with French, Danish, Swedish, Austrian and Portuguese equivalents. British ships ran 1,100–1,400 tons burden. They carried substantial armament against pirates and privateers, which is why a merchant hull of the period is built to the proportions of a warship.

Solar and de Zwart worked the Dutch-Asiatic Shipping database, which records every VOC voyage made. **VOC ships were slow, and they did not get faster.** Mean passage to Batavia was 253 days in 1770–75 and 238 in 1783–92, and there is 'no significant trend' across the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries at all.

English East Indiamen did the same passage in 173 days. The gap is 60–80 days between two fleets sailing the same ocean in the same years, and it is a fact about the hulls and the standing orders, not about the wind: Dutch hull form was constrained by shallow inland waterways, copper sheathing was adopted late, and the sailing instructions were conservative.
vessels.cite: Solar & de Zwart, *International Journal of Maritime History* 29(4) (2017); Bruijn, Gaastra & Schöffer, *Dutch-Asiatic Shipping*.

Roughly half of all line-of-battle ships by 1800 were 74s: the point on the curve where enough guns met enough speed.

The manning ratio distinguishes a warship from any other vessel of the period. A merchantman carried one man per 20–30 tons; *Victory* carried one per 2.6. Guns need hands, and the Royal Navy went from 16,000 men in 1739 to 145,000 in 1813, roughly half the wartime lower deck pressed. Of about 103,000 deaths between 1793 and 1815, **81% were disease and accident, 13% shipwreck and fire, and 6% enemy action.**

vessels.text:
For three centuries the principal cargo carried across the Atlantic was people. An estimated 12.5 million were embarked and 10.7 million landed.

The between-decks of a slave ship was a designed space, drawn by naval architects and optimised for a quantity of human beings per ton, and the optimisation is legible in the numbers: mortality fell across three centuries not because conditions became humane but because passages got shorter and the loss of cargo was expensive.

The crew figure is the one that moved Parliament. Thomas Clarkson's evidence was drawn from muster rolls showing that about a fifth of the **crews** died too — a trade that killed the people who ran it at a rate comparable to the people it carried.

*The voyage database that records all of this is licensed for non-commercial use only, so this model cites it and does not republish it. The figures here are the published aggregates.*
vessels.cite: Eltis & Richardson, *Atlas of the Transatlantic Slave Trade*; SlaveVoyages.org (cited, not redistributed — CC BY-NC).

vessels.name: Wyoming
vessels.sub: the longest wooden ship ever built
rows: 110 m on deck, 140 m overall — beam 15.3 m, depth of hold 10 m
foundered off Cape Cod, 11 March 1924, all hands
vessels.text:
Wyoming was at or past the practical limit for a wooden hull: she worked in a seaway badly enough to need steam pumps continuously, and she was lost with all hands in 1924.

At 110 m on deck she was too long to hold herself straight. A wooden hull resists bending only through the friction and fastenings between thousands of separate timbers, and past a certain length the sea simply works them: her planks twisted and opened, and **she ran her pumps continuously to stay afloat**. Not in heavy weather — always.

She foundered in a gale off Cape Cod in 1924 with everyone aboard. Iron and steel did not replace wood because they were cheaper; they replaced it because a metal hull is one continuous member and a wooden one is a negotiation.

And the rig is the other half of the story. Six masts of gaff sail are worked entirely from the deck — nobody goes aloft to reef — so she carried 3,730 tons with **thirteen people**. A square-rigged ship of that tonnage wanted thirty.
vessels.cite: Wikipedia, *Wyoming (schooner)*, citing the Percy & Small yard records.

vessels.sub: the largest sailing ship ever built
rows: 147 m overall, 122 m between perpendiculars — beam 16.4 m

vessels.text:
She was the largest sailing ship ever built and among the last commercially viable ones. She was lost in 1910 after a collision with a cross-Channel steamer that misjudged her speed.

Five masts, all square-rigged — the only ship ever built that way. 6,806 m² of canvas driving 5,081 tons round Cape Horn with nitrate, on a route where steam still could not compete because there was nowhere to coal.

In November 1910 the cross-Channel steamer *Brighton* misjudged her speed and tried to cross her bows. Preussen was making 16 knots. She broke her keel going ashore near Dover and was never salvaged.

That is the ending sail actually got: not obsolescence, but a steamer in a hurry.
vessels.cite: Wikipedia, *Preussen (ship)*; Laeisz Flying-P line records.

six times the tonnage of any ship then afloat; unsurpassed for 40 years

vessels.text:
Brunel built a ship six times bigger than anything afloat, and there was no trade for her.

The engineering was sound and the reasoning was sound: coal is the constraint on steam, and a bigger hull carries proportionally more of it, so a big enough ship could reach Australia without refuelling. She could. Nobody wanted to go to Australia in those numbers.

She spent her career unprofitable and ended doing the one job that needed a hull that size: **laying the Atlantic telegraph cable**, 4,200 km of it in one bottom. No other ship on earth could hold it.

No ship exceeded her tonnage for forty years.
vessels.cite: Wikipedia, *SS Great Eastern*; Brunel's own calculations on the coal fraction.

vessels.text:
She was not built to be fast. Cunard had the speed record and White Star chose not to compete for it — Titanic was built for **size and comfort**, on the theory that passengers would rather cross well than quickly.

Her sixteen watertight compartments were real, and they were not enough for a reason of geometry rather than engineering: **the bulkheads stopped at D deck**. Water filling one compartment past that level simply flowed over the top into the next. She could float with four flooded. The iceberg opened five.

The lifeboat number was legal. The regulation scaled boats to a ship's TONNAGE and had last been written when the largest ship afloat was 10,000 tons.
vessels.cite: Wikipedia, *RMS Titanic*; British Wreck Commissioner's Inquiry, 1912.

vessels.name: Unmanned surface vessel
vessels.sub: nobody aboard — a rigid wing, and no canvas
rows: wind, wave and solar; diesel-electric on some hulls
months, limited by fouling and machinery, not by stores
fastest uncrewed Atlantic crossing, Bermuda to the UK, August 2019

German remote-controlled FL-boats in the First World War; US Navy target and minesweeping craft in the Second

vessels.text:
A vessel that operates on the surface without a crew aboard, across a range from remote control to full autonomy. Propulsion may be wind, wave or solar: a wave glider takes its drive from the motion of the sea itself, and a Saildrone from wind and sunlight.

Removing the crew changes the constraint. A crewed ship's endurance is set by food, water and human tolerance; take the crew off and the limits become fouling, machinery and power. A wind-and-solar hull can stay out for **months**, and the sea state that would be dangerous for a manned vessel is merely slow for one that cannot drown.

It is a strange place for this story to arrive. The whole history above is people solving the problem of getting themselves across an ocean — and the current answer, for a growing share of the work, is not to go.
vessels.cite: Wikipedia, *Unmanned surface vehicle*; Saildrone and NOAA survey programmes.

vessels.name: Clipper
rows: ⚠ **not a sailplan.** A clipper is a hull — fine lines built for speed. Clippers were schooners, brigs and brigantines as well as full-rigged ships
hull 64.8 m, beam 10.97 m, 963 gross register tons

composite after 1863 — iron framework, wooden planking

vessels.text:
The fastest commercial sailing ships ever built, and they were obsolete almost immediately.

The Suez Canal opened in 1869, the year *Cutty Sark* was launched. It cut London–Bombay from about 10,600 nautical miles to 6,200 — and **sail could not use it**, because there is no wind in a cut and towage was charged. So the clippers were driven onto the routes the canal did not help: Australian wool, and Chilean nitrate round the Horn. They were the best answer to a question that had just stopped being asked.

The rival record is worth the argument it causes. *Andrew Jackson*'s 89 days 4 hours in 1860 was measured pilot-to-pilot at the Farallones, after which she lay all night waiting for a pilot; Cutler put her anchor-to-anchor time at possibly 89 days 20 hours. The two figures are not commensurable.
vessels.cite: Cutler, *Greyhounds of the Sea*; Royal Museums Greenwich.

vessels.name: Ocean steamer
rows: paddle wheels — impractical in a seaway and abandoned for the screw; turbines from *Lusitania* and *Mauretania*; diesel and oil firing from the early 1930s
under 10 kn — twelve days and more

vessels.text:
An iron-hulled, screw-driven steamship on a scheduled ocean route. The figure that governs its range is not horsepower but **pounds of coal per horsepower-hour**, which fell about threefold between 1855 and 1890.

That is what made steam viable on long routes. At 1850s efficiency a ship crossing an ocean had to give up roughly half its deadweight to its own fuel; by 1890 it was 15–20%. Nothing about the engine's power mattered as much as how little coal it burned to make it.

Compound expansion (1854), triple expansion (A. C. Kirk, 1881), then the turbine and oil firing. Steam overtook sail on the British register around 1883.
vessels.cite: Griffiths, *Steam at Sea*; Kirk on triple expansion, 1881.

vessels.text:
A battleship carrying a uniform main battery of ten 12-inch guns and driven by steam turbines, completed at Portsmouth in a year and a day. Both features were already understood separately; putting them in one hull made every existing battleship in every navy second-rate at a stroke, and the type took her name.

The all-big-gun battery follows from gunnery rather than from ambition. Fire control works by observing the fall of shot and correcting, and that is only possible if every splash comes from a gun of the same calibre — a mixed battery gives you two sets of splashes and no way to tell which is which at the ranges the guns could already reach.

The heaviest battleship ever built, carrying the largest naval guns ever mounted: nine 46 cm rifles in three triple turrets, behind a belt of 410 mm and a turret face of 650 mm.

She was sunk on 7 April 1945 by carrier aircraft, having barely fired those guns at an enemy ship. The armour was proof against the shells it was designed against, and the attack came from above.

vessels.name: Supercarrier
vessels.sub: Gerald R. Ford class · the deck is the weapon
rows: 41 m at the waterline — but **78 m across the flight deck**
two A1B reactors, four shafts, in excess of 30 kn
vessels.text:
A nuclear-powered aircraft carrier of about 100,000 tons. Its waterline beam is 41 m and its flight deck is 78 m across, because the deck overhangs the hull on both sides — the two numbers describe different things and neither alone describes the ship.

The angled deck is the feature everything else depends on. A landing strip set a few degrees to port means a pilot who misses the arrestor wires flies off the bow and goes round again, instead of into the aircraft parked forward behind a crash barrier. The island is small and to starboard so the deck stays clear, and to starboard specifically because an aircraft going around swings to port.

Two reactors remove the constraint that shaped every warship before: a hull that no longer carries its own fuel can spend that volume and that range on aircraft instead.
vessels.cite: Wikipedia, *Gerald R. Ford-class aircraft carrier* (accessed 2026-08-03).

vessels.text:
The last chapter of this story is not about the sea at all. A modern container ship's route is set by **lock chambers and dredged channels** — numbers written down by engineers — rather than by anything the ocean does.

Panamax is not a ship. It is the inside dimension of a lock built in 1914, and for a century the world's fleet was designed around it: 294.13 m long, 32.31 m in the beam, because that is what fits. The 2016 expansion moved the number and the fleet moved with it.

Growth has now stopped, and it stopped on port depth and canal width rather than on anything to do with naval architecture.
vessels.cite: Levinson, *The Box* (2006); Panama Canal Authority vessel requirements; Suez Canal Authority.

vessels.sub: the ship that stopped the Suez Canal

Service speed is set by fuel price as much as by the hull — ships of this class slow-steam near 16 knots when bunkers are dear, which is why the routing figure and a schedule figure can honestly differ.

vessels.text:
Ever Given is a 20,124 TEU container ship built by Imabari Shipbuilding in 2018 and operated by Evergreen Marine. At 399.94 m she is a metre short of the 400 m at which some port and canal rules change, which is not a coincidence: the largest ships are built to the dimensions of the infrastructure that must accept them.

On the morning of 23 March 2021 she entered the Suez Canal southbound at about 13 knots in a sandstorm with gusts above 40 knots, sheered, and grounded diagonally across the channel at kilometre 151, wedging her bulbous bow into the eastern bank. The canal is single-lane along that stretch and there is no way past. She was refloated on 29 March after 163 hours, by dredging roughly 30,000 cubic metres from around the bow, fourteen tugs, and a spring tide.

By the time she moved, 369 ships were waiting at both ends. Around 12 per cent of world trade passes through the canal, and the alternative — round the Cape — adds about 9,000 km and ten days. The blockage is the clearest demonstration this model has of its own last chapter's argument: a modern route is set by the dimensions of dredged channels and lock chambers, and one hull athwart one of them stops a system that has no slack in it.
vessels.cite: Suez Canal Authority; Marine Accident Investigation Branch interim report, 2021.

vessels.text:
Azzam was delivered by Lürssen in 2013 for Sheikh Khalifa bin Zayed Al Nahyan and at 180.6 m remains the longest private motor yacht built. She is included here as the end point of a line the rest of this model traces: for most of history the largest and most advanced hulls afloat were built to carry cargo, fight, or explore, and their size was justified by what they returned.

Her engineering is not decorative. A combined diesel and gas turbine plant of roughly 94,000 shaft horsepower drives four waterjets to over 30 knots — faster than most warships of comparable displacement — and she draws only 4.3 m on that length, a deliberately shallow hull for Gulf and Red Sea waters that forced a very fine, wide, low-block form.

The type is a real category rather than a curiosity: yachts above 100 m are now built in numbers, and they sustain specialist yards, naval-architecture practices and a supply chain that overlaps with naval work.

The rig is a compromise for ice work: enough square sail to run before the westerlies, few enough yards that a small crew can handle her among floes, and an engine for calms and leads.

vessels.text:
Endurance was built at Framnæs in Sandefjord in 1912 as *Polaris*, for Arctic tourist cruising, and was designed for ice rather than merely strengthened against it: oak and Norwegian fir with greenheart sheathing, and a stem formed from a single baulk about 1.3 m thick. Shackleton bought her for the Imperial Trans-Antarctic Expedition of 1914.

She was beset in the Weddell Sea pack on 19 January 1915, one day's sail from her intended landing, and drifted with the ice for ten months. A ship built for ice can survive pressure from the sides; what destroyed her was being lifted and racked as floes converged. She was abandoned on 27 October and sank on 21 November 1915. All twenty-eight men survived, by boat to Elephant Island and then by an 800-nautical-mile passage in the 6.9 m *James Caird* to South Georgia.

The wreck was located on 5 March 2022 at 3,008 m, about four nautical miles from the position Frank Worsley recorded by sextant as she went down — a navigational fix taken from an ice floe with no land in sight, and vindicated after a century.
vessels.cite: Endurance22 expedition; Worsley's navigational log; Alexander, *The Endurance* (1998).

vessels.sub: the last ship built to cross, not to cruise

polar.rigNote: Four azimuthing pods, two fixed and two steerable, fed by diesel-electric plant with gas turbines for the top end — about 117 MW. Pods rather than shafts because a liner hull fine enough to hold 26 knots in a North Atlantic winter has no room for four shaft lines.

vessels.text:
Queen Mary 2 entered service in 2004 and is the only ocean liner still in scheduled service. The distinction from a cruise ship is structural rather than commercial. A liner is built to hold a schedule across the North Atlantic in winter, which requires speed in a seaway and a hull that can take it: she has a long, fine, flared bow with a real forecastle, shell plating up to about twice the thickness of a comparable cruise ship's, and a service speed of 26 knots against the 22 a cruise ship makes.

Her propulsion is four azimuthing pods, two fixed and two steerable, fed by diesel-electric and gas-turbine plant — an arrangement that gives her the power for the crossing without the shaft lines a hull of that fineness has no room for.

She is the last of the type. The transatlantic liner was killed by the jet within a decade of 1958, and everything built since for that water has been built to cruise. That one ship is still constructed to cross it is why she belongs at the end of this fleet.
vessels.cite: Cunard; Payne, *From Track to Trestle* and Chantiers de l'Atlantique specifications.

crabclaw.rigNote: Poor by modern standards, positive by ancient ones — and positive is the whole argument, because it is what lets a canoe beat back the way she came. Fastest on a broad reach, not before the wind.
crabclaw.rig: crab claw on a double hull

square.rigNote: The famous "six points" is 67.5° — and it is a HEADING. What she makes good is the figure above, and above force 4 she loses ground to leeward faster than she gains it.

lateen.rigNote: Better than a square rig, and by less than the textbooks claim — their 55–65° is a heading. The cost is manpower: tacking means walking the whole yard round the mast.

gaff.rigNote: Points high and is worked entirely from the deck — nobody goes aloft to reef a gaff sail. That is the whole economic argument for the rig: the crew, not the speed.

junk.rigNote: The battens do it: they make the sail self-reefing and let it set flat, so it beats a square rig to windward on a fraction of the crew — about 75–80% of Bermudan performance.

oar.rigNote: A galley goes where it likes and not far, and the figure above is her SAILING speed — the sail is for fair winds only. Under oar: 8.3 kn sprint, 5.4 kn cruise, and about 2.9 kn into a headwind with a metre of sea — measured on the reconstruction Olympias, which fell short of what the ancient sources imply and is thought to be ~10% too short in the hull.
oar.rig: oars, with a square sail for fair winds

steam.rigNote: Does not care about the wind. Its constraint is coal: the bunker fraction, not the weather, decides where it can go.

motor.rigNote: Weather is a delay, not a route.
